newsitem.title: CHINA: China corn sales seen depending on Japan buying.
newsitem.headline: China corn sales seen depending on Japan buying.

text.p: China's corn export programme, which could already total up to two million tonnes this year, may grind to a halt if Japan did not become a more active buyer, traders and diplomats said on Friday.
"Japan is the big question mark," a Western agriculture official said, echoing many regional traders polled by Reuters.
"If Japan can let bygones be bygones, that could see China selling another half a million tonnes," he said.

Japanese trade houses harboured memories of Chinese defaults on corn shipments destined for Japan, the traders and diplomats said. Beijing introduced a blanket ban on corn exports in December 1994 and suddenly resumed sales in January this year, they said.
"We've been very cautious since then," a source at a Japanese firm in Hong Kong said.
South Korea, the major buyer so far, was covered through to August, traders said.
If Japan, perceived as still in need of corn, did come to China, total Chinese sales for this year could rise to 2.5 million tonnes, the Western official said.
A source in Beijing said he could tally only 75,000 tonnes of corn sales to Japan since China came back to the market.
The Western official said China's total sales since the export programme began in January were around 1.8 million tonnes.

More bullish trading sources said the sales are around two million tonnes, with more than one million to South Korea, some to Malaysia and Indonesia and a small government-to-government sale to the Philippines.
On Wednesday, Japan's Mitsui & Co Ltd said it had bought 7,400 tonnes of feed corn from China for May and July shipment.
Some Japanese traders have said that if the Chinese price were right they would buy. Sources in the region wondered if the Mitsui purchase could see other Japanese houses following suit.
Chinese corn is now being offered free on board (FOB) at the northern port of Dalian at $135 a tonne.
A trader at a major Japanese firm in Hong Kong said she was receiving many inquiries.
"But we'd want a $10 discount on that price," she said. High levels of foreign material -- rocks, sticks, sand -- in the Chinese corn cost a lot to remove, she said.
"That alone justifies $125 (a tonne)," she said.
With China having sold its corn at up to $10 a tonne cheaper than the U.S. and Argentinian product, Japan was cutting off its nose to spite its face, one trader in Singapore said.
A U.S. diplomatic source in Seoul has estimated that South Korea's purchases of Chinese corn in the marketing year to October 1997 could total two million tonnes.
This would push China's commitments for the marketing year ending October 31 to close to 2.5 million tonnes.
After a record corn harvest in 1996 of 118 million tonnes, and the ban on corn exports, China's grain storage facilities in the north-eastern growing regions are bursting at the seams.
While the exports are seen as a way of easing the storage congestion, up to half a million tonnes of the commitments to date could have been done through unofficial channels, trading sources said.
This could lead to some problems with export documentation that could hold up the flow of the corn out of the country, they said. Some sources reported hearing of these problems already.
